## Proposition 9.22
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole will be even.

**Step 1.** Let there be as many odd numbers as we please, say A1, A2, A3, ..., A2n, and let their multitude be even.

**Step 2.** Since the multitude of odd numbers is even, by D7.6 it is divisible into two equal parts. Therefore the odd numbers can be arranged into pairs: (A1, A2), (A3, A4), ..., (A(2n-1), A2n), yielding n pairs.

**Step 3.** Consider any one pair, say Ai and Ai+1, both odd. By D7.7, each odd number differs by a unit from an even number. Therefore Ai = Bi + 1 where Bi is even, and Ai+1 = Ci + 1 where Ci is even.

**Step 4.** Then Ai + Ai+1 = Bi + Ci + 2 [by CN2, adding equals to equals]. Now Bi, Ci, and 2 are all even numbers (Bi and Ci by construction, and 2 because it is divisible into two equal parts, namely two units, satisfying D7.6). Therefore the sum Bi + Ci + 2 is a sum of even numbers, which is even by 9.21.

**Step 5.** Thus each pair of odd numbers sums to an even number. We therefore have n even numbers, namely the sums S1 = A1 + A2, S2 = A3 + A4, ..., Sn = A(2n-1) + A2n.

**Step 6.** The total sum A1 + A2 + A3 + ... + A2n equals S1 + S2 + ... + Sn, which is a sum of as many even numbers as we please. By 9.21, this sum is even.

**Step 7.** Therefore, if as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole is even. Q.E.D.

heath_proof_text: For let as many odd numbers as we please, AB, BC, CD, DE, even in multitude, be added together; I say that the whole AE is even. For, since each of the numbers AB, BC, CD, DE is odd, if an unit be subtracted from each, each of the remainders will be even; [VII. Def. 7] so that the sum of them will be even. [IX. 21] But the multitude of the units is also even. Therefore the whole AE is also even. [IX. 21]
